Worcester.housing_era: Worcester is famous for its triple-deckers — thousands of three-story wood-frame multifamily homes built for mill and factory workers — alongside Victorian homes on the West Side, brick apartment blocks, and postwar suburbs in Tatnuck and West Tatnuck. Worcester.wildlife_intro:
Worcester's triple-decker neighborhoods give it a wildlife profile unlike anywhere else in central Massachusetts. Raccoons and gray squirrels move through connected rooflines and old chimneys across Main South, Grafton Hill, and the Vernon Hill streets, bats roost in the Victorian homes of the West Side and in older apartment blocks, and skunks and opossums den under the porches that front nearly every triple-decker. Rats follow the Blackstone corridor and older commercial basements, and woodchucks work the city's hillsides and rail edges.

In a triple-decker, one family's attic problem is usually the whole building's, so our crew inspects all three floors' rooflines, removes animals on site under Massachusetts law, and seals every entry point. Work is handled by a MassWildlife-licensed Problem Animal Control agent, and we coordinate with owners and tenants so everyone knows the plan. Call us at the first thumping overhead — in these buildings, early exclusion protects three households at once.

faqs.a: Cost depends on the species, how the animal got in, and how much exclusion and cleanup the home needs, so our crew inspects first and explains the options before any work starts. Simple one-animal jobs cost less than bat exclusion or attic cleanup after a long stay. Call us for an assessment of your home.

faqs.q: Raccoons are in the attic of our Worcester triple-decker — who handles that?
faqs.a: The building owner should call us: in a triple-decker the rooflines connect, so our crew inspects the whole structure, removes the raccoons on site under Massachusetts rules — relocation is prohibited here — and seals every entry point across all floors. That whole-building approach is what keeps them from returning through a neighbor's soffit.

Our crew's Leominster work pairs removal with thorough sealing, because most homes here have a second and third entry waiting behind the first. Bats are a leading call in the older multifamily homes, raccoons and gray squirrels work the attics and chimneys, and skunks and opossums den under porches across the neighborhoods. Woodchucks work the gardens and sunny banks, beavers dam the Otter River tributaries and brook systems, and mice are a certainty each fall in the older housing stock.
